Fix an integer $n$. Congruence modulo $n$ is an equivalence relation on
$\mathbb Z$ by [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]. The
**congruence class of $a$ modulo $n$** is

$$[a]_n:=\{\,b\in\mathbb Z:b\equiv a\pmod n\,\},$$

and the **integers modulo $n$** form the quotient set

$$\mathbb Z/n:=\{\,[a]_n:a\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$

This is the quotient-set construction of [[def-equivalence-relation]]. By
[[lem-equivalence-classes-partition]], two classes are equal exactly when their
representatives are congruent:

$$[a]_n=[b]_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\equiv b\pmod n.$$

At $n=0$ each class is a singleton because congruence modulo $0$ is equality.
At $n=1$ there is one class, namely $\mathbb Z$ itself.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every class in $\mathbb Z/n$
([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) contains exactly one integer $r$ with
$0\le r<n$. Consequently the map

$$r\longmapsto[r]_n\qquad(0\le r<n)$$

is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $n$ to $\mathbb Z/n$, and
$|\mathbb Z/n|=n$. This includes $n=1$, where the only representative is $0$.
For $n=0$, the map $a\mapsto[a]_0$ is a bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, including $n=0$ and $n=1$. For classes in
$\mathbb Z/n$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) define

$$[a]_n+[b]_n:=[a+b]_n,\qquad [a]_n[b]_n:=[ab]_n.$$

These are binary operations in the sense of [[def-binary-operation]]. Indeed,
if $[a]_n=[a']_n$ and $[b]_n=[b']_n$, then
$a\equiv a'\pmod n$ and $b\equiv b'\pmod n$, so

$$a+b\equiv a'+b'\pmod n,\qquad ab\equiv a'b'\pmod n$$

by [[lem-congruence-respects-integer-arithmetic]]. Thus the two displayed
classes do not depend on the representatives chosen.

For $n=0$, every class is a singleton and these operations reproduce integer
addition and multiplication under the bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$. For
$n=1$, the quotient has one element, so $[0]_1=[1]_1$ and both operations are
the unique binary operation on a one-element set.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, with addition and multiplication as in
[[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]:

1. $(\mathbb Z/n,+,[0]_n)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), with
   $-[a]_n=[-a]_n$;
2. $(\mathbb Z/n,\cdot,[1]_n)$ is a commutative monoid
   ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]);
3. multiplication distributes over addition on both sides.

The assertions include $n=0$ and $n=1$. At $n=1$, the two distinguished
identities coincide because $[0]_1=[1]_1$.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Then

$$\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\begin{cases}N,&k\equiv\ell\pmod N,\\\\ 0,&k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N.\end{cases}$$

At $N=1$ the congruence holds for all $k,\ell$ and the sum is $1$. The sum is the finite sum of the complex family $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}$ over the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and $N$ on the right is the natural number $N$ read in $\mathbb C$ as the additive multiple $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$, that is, the value at $N$ of the canonical embedding $\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]).

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\Lambda_{d,L}$ and put $a_j=\widetilde x_j$. By [F1]–[F2], the $j$th representative of $x+e_j$ is $a_j+1-L\epsilon_j$, where $\epsilon_j=1$ if $a_j=L-1$ and $0$ otherwise; the $j$th representative of $x-e_j$ is $a_j-1+L\eta_j$, where $\eta_j=1$ if $a_j=0$ and $0$ otherwise. All other representatives are unchanged. Substitution into the definition of $\chi_r$, followed by the exponential addition law and $\exp(2\pi i n)=1$ for integers $n$ from [F5], gives $\chi_r(x+e_j)=e^{2\pi i r_j/L}\chi_r(x)$ and $\chi_r(x-e_j)=e^{-2\pi i r_j/L}\chi_r(x)$. This also holds for $L=1$ and $L=2$.

For $r,s\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, finite-sum factorization [F4] and the conjugation identity [F8] give $\langle\chi_r,\chi_s\rangle=\prod_{j=1}^d L^{-1}\sum_{u=0}^{L-1}e^{2\pi i(r_j-s_j)u/L}$. By [F1], distinct canonical representatives are incongruent modulo $L$, so [F3] makes each factor $1$ when $r_j=s_j$ and $0$ otherwise. This is the inner-product identity stated above.

Substituting the shift identities of step 1.1 into $-\Delta$ gives $-\Delta\chi_r=\sum_{j=1}^d(2-e^{2\pi i r_j/L}-e^{-2\pi i r_j/L})\chi_r$. By [F6]–[F7], each coefficient equals $2-2\cos(2\pi r_j/L)=4\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)$, proving the eigenvalue formula.

For any $f:\Lambda_{d,L}\to\mathbb C$, set $\widehat f(r)=L^{-d}\sum_{y\in\Lambda_{d,L}}f(y)\overline{\chi_r(y)}$. By [F4] and [F8], the frequency sum factors as $\sum_r\chi_r(x)\overline{\chi_r(y)}=\prod_{j=1}^d\sum_{r_j=0}^{L-1}e^{2\pi i r_j(\widetilde x_j-\widetilde y_j)/L}$. The canonical-representative theorem [F1] and orthogonality [F3] make this product $L^d$ if $x=y$ in $\Lambda_{d,L}$ and $0$ otherwise. Therefore $\sum_r\widehat f(r)\chi_r(x)=L^{-d}\sum_y f(y)\sum_r\chi_r(x)\overline{\chi_r(y)}=f(x)$ for every $x$. If a linear combination $\sum_r c_r\chi_r$ vanishes, taking its inner product with $\chi_s$ and applying step 1.2 gives $c_s=0$ for each $s$, so the expansion is unique.

For every real $f$, the translations $x\mapsto x+e_j$ are bijections with inverses $x\mapsto x-e_j$, so reindexing the finite sums [F4] gives $\sum_xf(x)(-\Delta f)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_x(f(x+e_j)-f(x))^2\ge0$. Thus $-\Delta$ is positive semidefinite; its matrix is symmetric because every shift term is paired with its inverse shift. For nonzero $f$, $$f^{\mathsf T}(m^2I+\kappa(-\Delta))f=m^2\sum_xf(x)^2+\kappa\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_x(f(x+e_j)-f(x))^2>0,$$ since $m^2>0$ and $\kappa>0$. By steps 2.1 and 2.2, the spanning functions $\chi_r$ satisfy the eigenvalue equations in the Statement, so the combined operator has the displayed eigenvalues.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function

   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$

   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ (Finite sums and finite products, by recursion). Then $P$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}K_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix} =x^{\mathsf T}K_jx+(y+C_j^{-1}B_j^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}C_j(y+C_j^{-1}B_j^{\mathsf T}x).$$

- an integer $N\ge1$ and a real matrix $K_0\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ satisfying $K_0^{\mathsf T}=K_0$ and $v^{\mathsf T}K_0v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^N$.   $$R_0=\{1,\ldots,N\}\supseteq R_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq R_q,$$
  each given in increasing coordinate order.

2. If $E_j\ne\varnothing$, reorder the current coordinates as the increasing list of $R_j$ followed by the increasing list of $E_j$, and write the correspondingly permuted matrix
   $$K_{j-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A_j&B_j\\B_j^{\mathsf T}&C_j\end{pmatrix}.$$
   Solve the nonsingular system $C_jX_j=B_j^{\mathsf T}$, set
   $$K_j:=A_j-B_jX_j,\qquad \ell_j:=\frac{|E_j|}{2}\ln(2\pi)-\frac12\ln(\det C_j).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $n\ge1$, let $K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite, and let $\beta>0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $K_j,C_j,\ell_j$ be the algorithm outputs. At each stage write $E_j=R_{j-1}\setminus R_j$, and use the empty-set conventions of the algorithm. Then the algorithm terminates after $q$ stages, every nonempty retained precision $K_j$ is positive definite, and for every fixed retained vector $x\in\mathbb R^{R_q}$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^{\bigcup_{j=1}^q E_j}}\exp\!\left(-\frac12 \widetilde z(x,y)^{\mathsf T}K_0\widetilde z(x,y)\right)\,d\lambda(y)
=\exp\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^q\ell_j\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac12x^{\mathsf T}K_qx\right),$$

where $y$ lists the eliminated coordinates in increasing order, $\widetilde z(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{R_0}$ is the unique full coordinate vector agreeing with $x$ on $R_q$ and with $y$ on $R_0\setminus R_q$, and $\lambda$ is Euclidean Lebesgue measure in that finite-dimensional space. If $R_q\ne\varnothing$, the normalized marginal law of the retained coordinates under $\gamma_{K_0}$ is exactly $\gamma_{K_q}$; if $R_q=\varnothing$, the final retained space is the singleton $\mathbb R^0$ and the identity gives $Z_{K_0}=\exp(\sum_j\ell_j)$. In all cases,

$$\ln Z_{K_0}=\sum_{j=1}^q\ell_j+\ln Z_{K_q},$$

with $Z_{K_q}=1$ under the empty-space convention. These are exact finite-dimensional Gaussian identities and make no approximation or empirical claim.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$. For $N\ge1$, a real symmetric positive-definite matrix $K\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ (meaning $z^{\mathsf T}Kz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^N$) defines the finite centered Gaussian probability $\gamma_K$ on $\mathbb R^N$ by

$$Z_K:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2}\,d\lambda_N(z),\qquad \gamma_K(dz):=Z_K^{-1}e^{-z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2}\,d\lambda_N(z).$$

Under the stated Axiom of Countable Choice, $Z_K=(2\pi)^{N/2}(\det K)^{-1/2}$, $\mathbb E_{\gamma_K}[z]=0$, and $\operatorname{Cov}_{\gamma_K}(z)=K^{-1}$; these identities are the positive-quadratic-form Gaussian theorem of the mathematical supplier. Here $K$ is called the precision matrix because it appears in the quadratic exponent, and the covariance is its inverse. For $N=0$, define $\mathbb R^0$ to be the singleton containing the empty vector and define $\gamma_{\varnothing}$ to put mass one on that point; its partition factor and empty determinant are both $1$.

The variables $z_i$ and exponent $z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2$ are dimensionless in this mathematical definition. Consequently the remaining part is $n\sum_i x_i^2+\sum_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)^2$, which is positive when $x\ne0$; when $x=0$ and $(x,y)\ne0$, the first square is $y^2>0$. Hence $K_n$ is symmetric positive definite and the Gaussian law is defined by [F2].

$$2nI_n-\mathbf1_n[1]^{-1}\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}=2nI_n-\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}.$$
